edits.old: Paragraph 2 of the 1863 Wajib-ul-arz stated that co-sharers would partition according to Khewat shares or through the Patwari with Panchayat consent, and prohibited new cultivation (abadi) without all biswadars' consent [S238d7f39e142].
edits.new: Paragraph 2 of the 1863 Wajib-ul-arz described the mode of partition if desired by co-sharers, stating they would do so themselves in accordance with their shares shown in the Khewat papers or through the village Patwari in the presence of the Panchayat of the brotherhood, and prohibited new cultivation (abadi) without all biswadars' consent [S238d7f39e142].
edits.reason: Clarifies that Paragraph 2 describes the procedure for partition 'if desired' rather than establishing an unrestricted right, aligning with the source text which states 'When we, the co-sharers want to partition it...'

not_changed.reason: The draft date 'September 28, 1861' is supported by Source S417aaf0285ac ('September 28, 186 1'), despite a discrepancy with another source. No correction required based on available evidence.

Attribution of denied partition suits to the 1872-79 Settlement period is consistent with the chronological flow and subsequent litigation history (1890 applications). Source ambiguity does not justify changing the draft's reasonable inference.
The draft already includes the High Court's finding that the agreement was binding only while Settlements were in force and ceased upon expiry, as per Source S4b2b3a6e0136. No omission exists.

Attribution of the adverse possession argument to the Appellants (plaintiffs) is correct, as Dr. Tek Chand represented the appellants who lost in the High Court, per Source S869d8c8c61ea and procedural context.
The draft accurately reflects the Chief Court's ruling that the five sons of Dalmir could separate inter se but other co-sharers could not, per Source Sc2d688a625ac.
